mainTopic: Who is liable when someone walks into danger; paying only the difference when oxen and people injure each other; and whether the injured owner is a creditor or a partner in the goring ox.
overview: This amud finishes a discussion about a craftsman whose work hurt someone in his shop. The גמרא explains that a master may rely on his apprentice to obey a warning, because the apprentice fears him. רב זביד in the name of רבא then places רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, 'exempt from גלות but liable for four payments,' on the case of a person who sticks his head into the path of a thrown stone. The גמרא compares the two versions. Next, a ברייתא brings a dispute about workers who are hurt by the owner's animals when they come to collect their pay. The גמרא explains that the dispute turns on whether the owner's answer of "אִין" at the gate means "come in" or "wait there." A new משנה then teaches how payment works when oxen and people injure each other: only the difference between the two injuries is paid. In that משנה, רבי עקיבא holds that a תם ox that hurts a person pays full damages, and the גמרא brings the פסוקים each side relies on. Finally, a משנה about a cheap ox killing an expensive one leads to the argument between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא over whether the injured owner is a creditor or a partner. רבא's question about the damager selling the ox continues on the next amud.

steps.title: An apprentice fears his master, but a stranger does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers why the craftsman is treated differently when the one hurt is his own apprentice: the apprentice is afraid of his master and obeys him, while another person does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another person is not afraid of the craftsman, but this apprentice is afraid of his master.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an answer to a question from the earlier discussion. It explains why a craftsman can trust that his apprentice obeyed him, but cannot trust a stranger the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the master tells his apprentice to leave, he can assume the apprentice listened, because the apprentice fears him. So if the apprentice stayed anyway and was killed, the master is not to blame. A stranger has no such fear, so the craftsman cannot simply assume the stranger left.

keyTerms.meaning: Another person, meaning a stranger who is not the craftsman's apprentice
He does not have / he has

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the law looks at whether it is reasonable to assume a warning was obeyed. The relationship between the people affects who is to blame.

phrases.english: Another person does not have fear of his master,
phrases.notes: "His master" here means the craftsman. A stranger is not under the craftsman's authority, so he may ignore a warning.

phrases.english: this one has fear of his master.
phrases.notes: "This one" is the apprentice from the case just discussed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a contrast from the previous part of the sugya, which is not included in this section, between an apprentice and a stranger.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by the relationship between the people
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might have thought the apprentice and a stranger should be treated the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: The apprentice fears his master and will obey, so the master may rely on his warning. A stranger will not necessarily obey.

steps.title: A second version: the verse 'and finds' and the case of the stone
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says the ruling of רבי יוסי בר חנינא was taught on a different ברייתא. That ברייתא learns from the word 'and finds' that someone who puts himself in harm's way is excluded. On that basis, רבי אליעזר בן יעקב rules that a person who sticks his head out and is hit by a stone is the cause, so the thrower is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד, in the name of רבא, taught the ruling on this: 'And finds' excludes one who puts himself there. From here רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said: If a stone left someone's hand, and another person stuck out his head and was hit by it, the thrower is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of where רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling belongs. Here it sets up the new ברייתא, and the ruling itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about accidental killing says the axe-head 'finds' the victim. That suggests the victim was already in place. If the victim moved himself into the path, the killer is exempt from גלות. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב applies this to a stone already flying when someone pushes his head into its path.

keyTerms.meaning: He teaches it on this, meaning he attaches the ruling to this source
'And finds,' a word from the פסוק about accidental killing
One who places himself, putting himself into danger

steps.confusionAlert: רב זביד is not adding a new ruling. He is moving רבי יוסי בר חנינא's same ruling onto a different case.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid, in the name of Rava,
teaches it on this:
phrases.notes: "It" is רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, which comes again in the next step.

phrases.english: "And finds" excludes one who places himself there.
phrases.notes: דברים 19:5

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב:
phrases.english: From here Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said:
One from whose hand a stone went out,

phrases.aramaic: וְהוֹצִיא הַלָּה אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ וְקִיבְּלָהּ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and the other person stuck out his head and received it is exempt.
phrases.notes: The thrower is exempt from גלות, because the victim put himself in the stone's path.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא מַתְנֵי לַהּ אַהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different placement for רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, which earlier in the sugya was attached to the carpenter's-shop case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Based on 'and finds,' someone who puts himself into the path of harm excludes the one who caused it from גלות. A thrower whose stone hits a head that was stuck out into its path is exempt.

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר חנינא: no exile, but four payments
steps.stepSummary: In רב זביד's version, רבי יוסי בר חנינא says about the stone case: the thrower is exempt from גלות, but he must still pay four types of injury payments.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: He is exempt from exile, but liable for four payments.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, now attached to the stone case. It limits the exemption to גלות only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said 'exempt,' and רבי יוסי בר חנינא explains that this means exempt from גלות. If the victim was only injured, the thrower still owes four payments for hurting him. So, in this version, the victim's moving into the path does not erase money liability.

keyTerms.meaning: Exile to a city of refuge for an accidental killer
Four things, here meaning four of the payments for injuring a person

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
He is exempt from exile,
and liable for four things.
phrases.notes: These are four of the injury payments: damage, pain, medical costs, and lost work time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא: פָּטוּר מִגָּלוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב זביד's version by giving the ruling that is attached to the stone ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the stone case, the thrower is exempt from גלות but must pay four injury payments.

steps.title: Comparing the two versions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains how the two versions differ in practice. Whoever puts the ruling on the stone case would surely also apply it to the carpenter's case. Whoever puts it only on the carpenter's case holds that the stone thrower is fully exempt, even from payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever teaches it on this case would apply it even more so to the first case. But whoever teaches it on the first case holds that in this case he is completely exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up the practical difference between the two versions of רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the stone case the victim actively pushed his head into danger, so he carries more of the blame than the person in the carpenter's shop. So if the thrower still pays in the stone case, the carpenter certainly pays. But if the ruling was said only on the carpenter's case, the stone thrower owes nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so, an even stronger case
The first one, the earlier case
Completely exempt, from both גלות and payment

steps.whatToRemember: Version 1, on the carpenter's case: the stone thrower is fully exempt. Version 2, רב זביד's version on the stone case: the stone thrower pays four payments, and the carpenter surely does too.

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on this
phrases.notes: "This" is the stone case. "The first" is the carpenter's-shop case from earlier.

phrases.english: would all the more so apply it to the first one;
but the one who teaches it on the first one
holds that in this case he is completely exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ אַהָא – כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַקַּמַּיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares רב זביד's version with the earlier placement of the same ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two versions disagree only about the stone case. Both agree the carpenter pays four payments. Under the first version, the stone thrower is completely exempt.

steps.title: Workers hurt by the owner's animals while collecting pay
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: workers came to the owner's property to collect their wages and were gored by his ox or bitten by his dog, and one died. The first opinion says the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Workers came to collect their wages from the homeowner, and the homeowner's ox gored them or his dog bit them, and one died. The owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about workers who are hurt while coming to get paid. The first opinion rules the owner is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case asks whether the workers count as people who entered the owner's property with permission. The first opinion exempts the owner. From the next opinion's reasoning, this seems to be because they came in on their own and not with permission.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught, introducing a ברייתא

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: פּוֹעֲלִים שֶׁבָּאוּ לִתְבּוֹעַ שְׂכָרָן מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת,
phrases.english: Workers who came to claim their wages from the homeowner,
and the homeowner's ox gored them
or the homeowner's dog bit them,
and one died — he is exempt.
phrases.notes: "He" is the homeowner.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: פּוֹעֲלִים שֶׁבָּאוּ לִתְבּוֹעַ שְׂכָרָן מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new ברייתא on a related theme: harm to someone who entered another person's property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First opinion: the homeowner is exempt when his animals kill workers who came to collect their wages.

steps.title: Others: workers are allowed to come for their pay
steps.stepSummary: אחרים disagree. Workers have the right to come and collect their wages, so they are not trespassers, and the owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say: Workers are allowed to claim their wages from the homeowner.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a dissenting opinion. אחרים say the workers had every right to be there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying the workers are 'permitted,' אחרים treat them like people who entered with permission. The owner should have expected them, so he is responsible for what his animals did. The whole dispute depends on whether coming to collect pay counts as permission to enter.
steps.whatToRemember: First opinion: the workers count as entering without permission, so the owner is exempt. אחרים: workers have a right to come for their pay, so the owner is liable.

phrases.english: Others say:

phrases.aramaic: רַשָּׁאִין פּוֹעֲלִין לִתְבּוֹעַ שְׂכָרָן מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: Workers are permitted to claim their wages from the homeowner.
phrases.notes: He means they are allowed to be there, so the owner is liable for the harm.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Workers coming for their wages have a right to enter, so the owner is liable for harm from his animals.

steps.title: What exact case are they arguing about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets up a two-sided problem. If the owner is easy to find in town, why would אחרים make him liable? If he can only be found at home, why would the תנא קמא exempt him?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the owner can be found in town, what is the reason of אחרים? If he can only be found at home, what is the reason of the תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is trying to pin down the exact case in the argument from steps 5 and 6. It shows that each obvious version of the case makes one of the two opinions hard to understand. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner is easy to find in town, the workers had no need to enter his yard, so they look like trespassers. Then why would אחרים hold him liable? If he can only be found at home, the workers had to come there, so why would the תנא קמא exempt him? Neither simple case works for both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What exactly are the circumstances?
The first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If the owner can be found in town,
what is the reason of the אחרים (who make him liable)?
If he can be found only at home,
what is the reason of the first תנא (who exempts him)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the case behind the argument between the תנא קמא and אחרים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument between the תנא קמא (exempt) and אחרים (liable) about workers hurt in the owner's yard.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each simple version of the case makes one opinion look unreasonable, so the argument seems to have no case where it works.

steps.title: The owner said "yes" at the gate
steps.stepSummary: The case is an owner who is sometimes in town and sometimes not. The workers called at his gate and he answered "אִין". One side reads that as "come in" and the other as "stay where you are."
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is a man who is sometimes found and sometimes not. They called at the gate and he said "yes." One master holds "yes" means "come in." The other master holds "yes" means "stay where you are."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by giving a middle case. The real argument is about what the owner meant when he said "yes."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the owner is not reliably found in town, the workers had a fair reason to come to his house. So the argument is no longer about whether they may come at all. It is about whether his "yes" gave them permission to enter. אחרים hear it as "come in," so he is liable. The תנא קמא hears it as "wait there, I'm coming," so he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (introduces the real case)

steps.whyThisMatters: The whole question of liability turns on how one short word is understood. That is a clear example of how permission to enter decides whether someone counts as a trespasser.

phrases.english: No, it is needed only
for a man who is sometimes found in town and sometimes not,
and they called to him at the gate
and he said to them, "Yes."
One master holds that "yes" means "come in."
phrases.notes: This is אחרים, which is why they make the owner liable.

phrases.english: And the other master holds that "yes" means "stand where you are."
phrases.notes: This is the תנא קמא. He means "wait there, I'll come out to you."

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, בְּגַבְרָא דִּשְׁכִיחַ וְלָא שְׁכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided question by giving a middle case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the argument in a specific middle case and reframes it as a dispute over what a word means.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument seemed to be about whether workers may come to the house at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees they may come. The argument is whether "אִין" gave permission to enter.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows that "yes" means "stay there"
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a worker who came in to collect his wages and was hurt by the owner's ox or dog gets nothing, even though he came in with permission. The גמרא asks how that makes sense and concludes that he only had a "yes" at the gate, which means "stay there."
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports the view that "yes" means "stand where you are." It teaches: a worker who entered to claim his wages from the owner, and the owner's ox gored him or his dog bit him, the owner is exempt, even though he entered with permission. Why exempt? Must it not be that he called at the gate and the owner said "yes"? Learn from this that "yes" means "stand where you are."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support one side of the argument. It reads the ברייתא closely to show that "yes" means "stay where you are."
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself: if he came in with permission, why is the owner exempt? The only way it makes sense is that his "permission" was just a "yes" called back at the gate. That "yes" did not really invite him in, so he still counts as entering without real permission.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא is taught that supports the one who says...
Rather, is it not that...? (introduces the only reading that works)
Learn from it, conclude from it

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא supports the תנא קמא: an owner who only answers "yes" from inside has not invited the worker in, so he is not liable when his animal hurts him.
steps.confusionAlert: "Entered with permission" in this ברייתא does not mean a real invitation inside. The גמרא's point is that the only "permission" here was the word "yes" at the gate.

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא like the one who says
that "yes" means "stand where you are,"
as it is taught:

phrases.aramaic: פּוֹעֵל שֶׁנִּכְנַס לִתְבּוֹעַ שְׂכָרוֹ מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת,
phrases.english: A worker who entered to claim his wages from the homeowner,
and the homeowner's ox gored him
or his dog bit him,
he is exempt,
even though the worker entered with permission.
Why is he exempt?
Rather, is it not that the worker called at the gate,
and the owner said to him, "Yes"?
So learn from it
that "yes" means "stand where you are."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for one side of the argument described in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The view that "אִין" means "stand where you are" (the תנא קמא).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that exempts the owner even though the worker entered "with permission," which only makes sense if the permission was a mere "yes" at the gate.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: "אִין" called from inside means "wait where you are," not "come in."

steps.title: Two oxen that injured each other
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: when two oxen injure each other, the owners pay only on the difference between the two injuries. With two תם oxen that is half the difference; with two מועד oxen it is the full difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two תם oxen that injured each other: they pay half damages on the difference. If both are מועד: they pay full damages on the difference.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new topic: two oxen that hurt each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of each owner paying the other separately, the two injuries are measured and offset against each other. Only the leftover amount is paid. A תם ox pays half damages and a מועד ox pays full damages, so the payment on that leftover follows the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox not yet known as a gorer; its owner pays half damages
An ox known as a gorer; its owner pays full damages

phrases.english: משנה:
Two תם oxen
that injured each other,
they pay half damages on the difference.
phrases.notes: You compare the two injuries, and the owner of the ox that did more damage pays half of the extra.

phrases.english: If both are מועד,
they pay full damages on the difference.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁנֵי שְׁווֹרִין תַּמִּין שֶׁחָבְלוּ זֶה אֶת זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When oxen injure each other, payment is only on the difference: half for תם, full for מועד.

steps.title: One innocuous ox and one forewarned ox injure each other
steps.stepSummary: If a מועד ox did more damage to a תם ox, its owner pays the full difference. If the תם did more damage to the מועד, its owner pays half the difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one ox is תם and one is מועד: when the מועד did more damage to the תם, its owner pays full damages on the extra amount. When the תם did more damage to the מועד, its owner pays half damages on the extra amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues its list from the last step and now covers a mixed pair: one תם ox and one מועד ox that hurt each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two injuries still cancel each other out, and only the extra damage is paid. The rate depends on the ox that caused the bigger injury. A מועד ox pays full and a תם ox pays half.

keyTerms.meaning: The extra amount: how much bigger one injury is than the other
A forewarned ox that damaged an innocuous ox
An innocuous ox that damaged a forewarned ox

phrases.english: If one is innocuous and one is forewarned:

phrases.aramaic: מוּעָד בַּתָּם מְשַׁלֵּם בַּמּוֹתָר נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם,
phrases.english: if the forewarned did more damage to the innocuous, its owner pays full damages on the difference;
if the innocuous did more damage to the forewarned,
its owner pays half damages on the difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the mixed case (one תם and one מועד) to the two-תם and two-מועד cases from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a mixed pair, the side that caused more damage pays on the difference at its own rate: full for a מועד, half for a תם.

steps.title: Two people who injure each other
steps.stepSummary: Two people who hurt each other: the one who did more damage pays the full difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same applies to two people who hurt each other. The one who caused more damage pays full damages on the extra amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the same "pay only the difference" rule to two people who hurt each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person always pays full damages, because a person is treated like a מועד (אדם מועד לעולם). So there is no half rate here. The one who did more damage pays the full difference.

keyTerms.meaning: And likewise: the same rule carries over

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים שֶׁחָבְלוּ זֶה בָּזֶה –
phrases.english: And likewise, two people who injured each other
pay full damages on the difference.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים שֶׁחָבְלוּ זֶה בָּזֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves the same rule from oxen to people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Between two people, the one who did more damage pays the full difference.

steps.title: A person and an ox injure each other
steps.stepSummary: A person and a מועד ox: whoever did more damage pays the full difference. A person and a תם ox: the person pays full if he did more damage, and the תם ox's owner pays half if the ox did more damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person and a מועד ox that hurt each other: whichever did more damage pays full damages on the extra amount. A person and a תם ox that hurt each other: if the person did more damage, he pays full damages on the extra amount. If the תם ox did more damage, its owner pays half damages on the extra amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now mixes people and oxen. It gives the rule for a person against a מועד ox and for a person against a תם ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person and a מועד ox both pay full, so whichever side did more damage pays the full difference. With a תם ox the rate depends on who did more damage: full if it was the person, half if it was the ox. This half-rate ruling is the view of the תנא קמא, and רבי עקיבא will argue with it next.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who damaged an innocuous ox
An innocuous ox that damaged a person

phrases.english: A person against a forewarned ox, and a forewarned ox against a person:
the one who did more pays full damages on the difference.
A person against an innocuous ox, and an innocuous ox against a person:

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם בַּתָּם מְשַׁלֵּם בַּמּוֹתָר נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם,
phrases.english: if the person did more to the innocuous ox, he pays full damages on the difference;

phrases.aramaic: תָּם בָּאָדָם מְשַׁלֵּם בַּמּוֹתָר חֲצִי נֶזֶק.
phrases.english: if the innocuous ox did more to the person, its owner pays half damages on the difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines the ox cases and the person case into mixed person-and-ox cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תם ox that did more damage to a person pays only half on the difference. A person or a מועד ox pays full.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: an innocuous ox that hurts a person pays full
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא holds that even a תם ox that injured a person pays the full difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: even a תם ox that hurt a person pays full damages on the extra amount.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא disagrees with the last ruling of the תנא קמא about a תם ox that hurt a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, the half-damage rule for a תם ox does not apply when it hurts a person. The גמרא will show in step 16 that he learns this from the words ״כמשפט הזה״. The only disagreement is about a תם ox hurting a person, and nobody here disputes the other cases.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who disagrees with the תנא קמא here

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is not saying a תם ox stops being a תם. It is still a תם ox. He only says that when it hurts a person, its owner pays the full amount.

phrases.english: רבי עקיבא says:
Even an innocuous ox that injured a person
pays full damages on the difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the half-damage ruling for a תם ox that hurt a person in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי עקיבא, a תם ox that injures a person pays full damages.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns from a פסוק: ox against person is like ox against ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא. It learns from ״כמשפט הזה יעשה לו״ that an ox hurting a person follows the rules of an ox hurting an ox: a תם pays half and a מועד pays full.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: "According to this judgment shall it be done to him." Just as the law is for an ox that hurts an ox, so is the law for an ox that hurts a person. For an ox that hurts an ox, a תם pays half damages and a מועד pays full damages. So too for an ox that hurts a person, a תם pays half damages and a מועד pays full damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by bringing a ברייתא that finds a source in a פסוק for the תנא קמא's view against רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words ״כמשפט הזה״ ("like this judgment") are read as comparing an ox that hurts a person to an ox that hurts an ox. Since a תם ox that hurts an ox pays only half, a תם ox that hurts a person also pays only half. This gives the תנא קמא a source and sets up the question of how רבי עקיבא reads the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
According to this judgment shall it be done to him
Just as ... so too: the form of a comparison

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the תנא קמא's half-damage ruling, so רבי עקיבא's view now has to be squared with this פסוק.
steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא learns from ״כמשפט הזה״ that an ox hurting a person is judged exactly like an ox hurting an ox: a תם pays half and a מועד pays full.

phrases.english: גמרא: The Rabbis taught:
"According to this judgment shall it be done to him":
phrases.notes: שמות 21:31

phrases.english: just as is the judgment of an ox against an ox,
so is the judgment of an ox against a person.
Just as with an ox against an ox,

phrases.aramaic: תָּם מְשַׁלֵּם חֲצִי נֶזֶק, וּמוּעָד נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם,
phrases.english: an innocuous one pays half damages and a forewarned one pays full damages,
so too with an ox against a person,

phrases.aramaic: תָּם מְשַׁלֵּם חֲצִי נֶזֶק, וּמוּעָד נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם.
phrases.english: an innocuous one pays half damages and a forewarned one pays full damages.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן כַּמִּשְׁפָּט הַזֶּה יֵעָשֶׂה לּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה by giving a source in a פסוק for the תנא קמא's ruling, against רבי עקיבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Based on ״כמשפט הזה״, an ox that hurts a person is treated like an ox that hurts an ox: a תם pays half and a מועד pays full.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: compare it to the lower verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא reads ״כמשפט הזה״ as pointing to the lower פסוק (the מועד), not the upper one (the תם).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: ״According to this judgment″ means like the lower verse, and not like the upper verse.
steps.whatsHappening: Within the same ברייתא, רבי עקיבא gives his own reading of ״כמשפט הזה״. He says an ox that hurts a person is judged like the lower פסוק, the case of a מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא in step 15 read the פסוק as copying both rules of ox-hurts-ox: half for a תם and full for a מועד. רבי עקיבא reads ״הזה״ as pointing only to the nearest פסוק, the מועד. So an ox that hurts a person always pays full damages. This is the source for his opinion in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the lower one (the later פסוק, about a מועד)
Like the upper one (the earlier פסוק, about a תם)
According to this judgment (the פסוק being read)

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
″According to this judgment″ means
like the lower one, and not like the upper one.
phrases.notes: The lower פסוק is the מועד case (שמות 21:29). The upper one is the תם case (שמות 21:28).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי עקיבא's competing reading of the same פסוק that the תנא קמא explained in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox that injures a person is compared to a מועד, so its owner pays full damages.

steps.title: Full payment, but only from the ox itself
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא limits the comparison. A תם that hurts a person pays full damages, but only from the ox's own body, not from the owner's best property.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think he pays from his best-quality property. So the פסוק says ״it shall be done to him/it″: he pays from its body, and he does not pay from his best-quality property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא continues and blocks a possible mistake. Even though the payment is full like a מועד, a תם ox pays only out of its own value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A real מועד pays from the owner's general property, even his best land. Someone could think the comparison to the מועד brings this rule along too. The word ״לו״ teaches that payment comes from the ox's body, the way a תם pays. So the amount is like a מועד, but the source of payment is like a תם.

keyTerms.meaning: From its body (from the value of the ox itself)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי עקיבא turns a תם into a full מועד. He takes only the full amount from the מועד. Payment still comes only from the ox's body, like a תם.

phrases.english: One might think he pays from his best-quality property,
therefore the verse says: ″It shall be done to him [it]″ —
phrases.notes: The word ״לו״ can also mean "it", so it is read as pointing to the ox.

phrases.english: he pays from its body,
and he does not pay from his best-quality property.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל מְשַׁלֵּם מִן הָעֲלִיָּיה, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the comparison made in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תם that injures a person pays full damages, but only up to the value of the ox's own body.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how רבי עקיבא's full-payment rule for a תם actually works in practice.

steps.title: Why do the רבנן need the word זה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן learn from the word ״זה״, since they do not use it the way רבי עקיבא does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן: why do I need the word ״this″?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the רבנן, the תנא קמא of step 15, and asks what the word ״זה״ teaches them. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא uses ״הזה״ to point to the lower פסוק. The רבנן compare to both cases, so for them ״כמשפט״ alone would have been enough. The extra word ״זה״ needs a job.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (what does this word teach?)
The Sages (here, the תנא קמא of the ברייתא)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis —
why do I need ″this″?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the opinion of step 15 deals with the word that רבי עקיבא used in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word ״זה״ teaches according to the רבנן.

steps.title: זה exempts from the four payments
steps.stepSummary: For the רבנן, ״זה״ teaches that an ox's owner is exempt from the four extra payments a person pays when he injures someone.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exempt him from the four things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן use ״זה״ to exempt the ox's owner from the four extra payments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״This judgment″ means only the judgment of an ox, that is, payment for the damage itself. The four extra payments that apply when a person injures someone do not apply when an ox does the injuring.

keyTerms.meaning: The four extra payments: pain, medical costs, lost work, embarrassment

phrases.english: To exempt him from the four things.
phrases.notes: These are the four extra payments a person who injures someone owes: pain, medical costs, lost work, and embarrassment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״זה״ teaches that an ox's owner does not pay the four extra payments.

steps.title: Where does רבי עקיבא learn the exemption?
steps.stepSummary: Since רבי עקיבא already used ״הזה״ for something else, the גמרא asks where he learns the exemption from the four payments.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי עקיבא: from where does he learn to exempt him from the four things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the opposite question. רבי עקיבא used the word for another lesson, so where does he get this exemption? It sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that an ox's owner does not pay the four payments. רבי עקיבא used ״הזה״ to point to the lower פסוק, so he needs a different source for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he know it?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Akiva —
exempting him from the four things,
from where does he derive it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא – לְפוֹטְרוֹ מֵאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 18: having found the רבנן's source, the גמרא looks for רבי עקיבא's.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי עקיבא's source for exempting an ox's owner from the four payments.

steps.title: A man injuring his fellow, not an ox
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא learns the exemption from ״איש כי יתן מום בעמיתו״: the four payments apply only when a person does the injuring.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from ״When a man injures his fellow″: a man injuring his fellow, and not an ox injuring his fellow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי עקיבא learns the exemption from a different פסוק, which speaks only about a person who injures someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק that is the source of the injury payments says ״איש״, a man. So those payments apply only when a person injures. When an ox injures, the owner pays only for the damage itself. Both opinions reach the same rule from different words.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא: an ox that hurts a person pays full damages, but only from the ox's body (לו). Everyone agrees there are no four extra payments. The רבנן learn it from ״זה״; רבי עקיבא learns it from ״איש בעמיתו״.

phrases.english: He derives it
from ″When a man injures his fellow″;
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:19

phrases.english: ″a man … his fellow″ —
and not an ox … his fellow.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵ״אִישׁ כִּי יִתֵּן מוּם בַּעֲמִיתוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From ״איש כי יתן מום בעמיתו״: the four payments apply only when a person injures, not when an ox does.

steps.title: Why the רבנן still need the word ״זה״
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן need ״זה״ because the פסוק ״איש כי יתן מום״ alone would only exempt the ox's owner from צער, not from ריפוי and שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why don't the רבנן learn it from that פסוק? If we only had that פסוק, I would think the ox's owner is exempt only from pain, but must still pay medical costs and lost work. So ״זה״ teaches us that he is exempt from all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the רבנן don't use רבי עקיבא's פסוק, and answers that this פסוק alone would not teach enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From ״איש כי יתן מום בעמיתו״ alone, we might exempt the ox's owner only from צער. Then ריפוי and שבת would still be owed. The רבנן need ״זה״ to show that the ox's owner pays none of the extra payments, only the damage itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for the pain of an injury
Payment for lost work while recovering
It teaches us (the extra word is needed to teach this)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that the owner of an ox does not pay the extra payments for injury. They only argue about which פסוק teaches it, and the רבנן explain why they need ״זה״ as well.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis? If it were from that verse,
phrases.notes: "That verse" is ״איש כי יתן מום בעמיתו״ from the step before.

phrases.english: I would have said: only pain is exempt,
but medical costs and lost work,
I would say he must pay him;
so it teaches us otherwise.
phrases.notes: "It" is the word ״זה״, which shows none of the extra payments apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the רבנן do not rely only on רבי עקיבא's פסוק from step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק ״איש כי יתן מום״ alone would exempt only צער, so ״זה״ is needed to exempt ריפוי and שבת as well.

steps.title: משנה: a cheap ox kills an expensive ox
steps.stepSummary: A שור תם worth 100 kills an ox worth 200, and the carcass is worthless. The injured owner takes the goring ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: An ox worth 100 gored an ox worth 200, and the dead ox's body is worth nothing. The owner of the dead ox takes the goring ox.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה gives a case: the damage is 200, half damages is 100, so the injured owner takes the whole goring ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שור תם pays half the damage, and only from its own body. Half of 200 is 100, which is exactly the goring ox's value, so the injured owner gets the entire ox. The משנה says he simply "takes" it, and the גמרא will ask whose view that is.

keyTerms.meaning: The body of the dead animal

phrases.english: Mishnah:
An ox worth a maneh (100)
that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth nothing —
he takes the ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָנֶה שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When half the damage equals the goring ox's value and the carcass is worthless, the injured owner takes the entire goring ox.

steps.title: Whose view is this משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא the משנה follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Whose opinion is our משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move by asking whose opinion the משנה follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the injured owner simply "takes the ox," as if it is already his. The גמרא wants to know which תנא holds this.

phrases.english: Gemara: Whose view is our Mishnah?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's opinion the משנה follows.

steps.title: It is רבי עקיבא, who says the ox is assigned right away
steps.stepSummary: The משנה follows רבי עקיבא, who says the ox is assigned right away, against רבי ישמעאל, who says it must be appraised in בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי עקיבא. As a ברייתא teaches: The ox is appraised in court; these are the words of רבי ישמעאל. רבי עקיבא says: The ox was assigned to the injured owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה follows רבי עקיבא, and quotes a ברייתא where he argues with רבי ישמעאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל says the goring ox must first be appraised in בית דין before payment. רבי עקיבא says the ox already belongs to the injured owner. That fits the משנה's simple wording "he takes the ox."

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Akiva.
As it was taught: The ox is appraised in court,
the words of Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Akiva says: The ox was assigned.
phrases.notes: He means the ox already belongs to the injured owner, with no more steps needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה follows רבי עקיבא, who holds the goring ox is assigned to the injured owner right away.

steps.title: What is the root of their argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what principle רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move by asking for the reason behind the two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know what each one rules, appraisal or immediate assignment. Now the גמרא wants the deeper principle that causes the difference.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the dispute quoted in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: Creditor or partner
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל sees the injured owner as a creditor owed money. רבי עקיבא sees him as a partner who owns part of the goring ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל holds: he is a creditor, and it is money that he is claiming from him. רבי עקיבא holds: they are partners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the root of the argument: is the injured owner owed money, or does he actually own part of the ox?
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ישמעאל, the injured owner is a בעל חוב who is only owed money, so בית דין must appraise the ox before he collects. For רבי עקיבא, from the moment of the goring the injured owner is a שותף in the goring ox itself, so it already belongs to him.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל: the injured owner is a בעל חוב owed money. רבי עקיבא: he is a שותף who owns part of the goring ox. The משנה follows רבי עקיבא.
steps.confusionAlert: Both agree a שור תם pays half damages from its own body. They only argue about the injured owner's status before payment: owed money, or already part owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: This creditor-or-partner idea is the key for the rest of the sugya, since it decides who owns the goring ox right after the damage.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: בַּעַל חוֹב הוּא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael holds: he is a creditor,
and it is money that he is claiming from him.
And Rabbi Akiva holds: they are partners.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: בַּעַל חוֹב הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי ישמעאל treats the injured owner as a creditor owed money. רבי עקיבא treats him as a partner in the goring ox.

steps.title: The פסוק the two תנאים read differently
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל reads 'ומכרו את השור החי' as a command to the בית דין. רבי עקיבא reads it as a command to the ניזק and the מזיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about this verse: 'They shall sell the live ox and divide its money.' רבי ישמעאל says the Torah is talking to the court. רבי עקיבא says the Torah is talking to the injured person and the one who caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows which פסוק each תנא's view comes from. It is finishing the answer about what they argue over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק is talking to the בית דין, nothing belongs to the ניזק until the court rules, so he is only a creditor. If the פסוק is talking to the owners themselves, the ox already belongs to both of them, so they are partners. This gives a source in the Torah for the creditor and partner views from step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: The Torah commands (literally, 'the Merciful One warns')
The one who caused the damage

steps.whyThisMatters: It ties the creditor and partner ideas to the wording of the Torah itself.

phrases.english: And they disagree about this verse:
"They shall sell the live ox
phrases.notes: שמות 21:35

phrases.english: and divide its money"
Rabbi Yishmael holds:
The Torah is commanding the court;
and Rabbi Akiva holds:
The Torah is commanding the injured party and the damager.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verse that the creditor and partner views of step 27 come from.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The disagreement comes from whom the פסוק is talking to: the court (רבי ישמעאל) or the two parties (רבי עקיבא).

steps.title: Asking for the practical difference
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the two views.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks when the two views would lead to a different result in real life. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both views agree that the ניזק ends up with the ox. So the גמרא wants a case where calling him a creditor or a partner actually changes the outcome.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the disagreement explained in steps 27 and 28 matters in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא would rule differently.

steps.title: If the injured party made the ox holy
steps.stepSummary: The difference is when the ניזק declared the goring ox הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is a case where the injured party made the ox holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the views differ if the ניזק tried to make the ox הקדש before the court acted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person can only make something הקדש if it belongs to him. For רבי עקיבא the ניזק already owns a share of the ox, so his הקדש works. For רבי ישמעאל he is only a creditor until בית דין acts, so the ox is not his yet and his הקדש does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: He made it holy (gave it to the בית המקדש)
There is a difference between them

steps.whatToRemember: Partner (רבי עקיבא) means the ניזק already owns part of the ox, so his הקדש works. Creditor (רבי ישמעאל) means he does not own it yet, so his הקדש does not work.

phrases.english: If the injured party made it holy
that is the difference between them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ניזק made the ox הקדש. It works for רבי עקיבא, who sees him as a partner, and not for רבי ישמעאל, who sees him as a creditor.

steps.title: What if the damager sold the ox?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רב נחמן: according to רבי ישמעאל, if the מזיק sold the ox, does the sale stand?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked רב נחמן: If the one who caused the damage sold the ox, what is the law according to רבי ישמעאל? Since רבי ישמעאל says the injured party is only a creditor who is owed money, maybe the sale works. Or perhaps...
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a new question about selling the ox under רבי ישמעאל's view. Here he gives the first side, that the sale works, and the other side is given in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי ישמעאל the ox still belongs to the מזיק, and the ניזק only has a claim for money. So it would seem the מזיק can sell his own ox. The words 'או דלמא' show that רבא also sees a reason it might not work.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps (brings in the other side of a question)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is about רבי ישמעאל only. For רבי עקיבא the ניזק already owns part of the ox, so the question is different.

phrases.english: Rava asked Rav Nachman:
If the damager sold it,
what is the law according to Rabbi Yishmael?
Since Rabbi Yishmael said
he is a creditor,
phrases.notes: "He" is the injured party, the one whose ox was killed.

phrases.english: and it is money that he is claiming from him,
it is sold;
or perhaps,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי ישמעאל's creditor view from steps 27 and 28 to ask a new question about the מזיק selling the ox.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, according to רבי ישמעאל, a sale of the goring ox by the מזיק stands, given that the ניזק is only a creditor.
